title: Putin’s biggest ally questions a key claim Russia uses to justify invasion of Ukraine | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Russia’s closest ally Belarus has questioned the logic behind Moscow’s claim over Ukrainian territory, likening it to Mongolia demanding to take over Russian lands.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has argued thatUkraine should be partof Russia because Kyiv was at the heart of the medieval federation known as the Ancient Rus.

Experts have long said this was – at best – an exercise in historical revisionism, but now even Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, who is usually hand in hand with Putin, has cast doubt on the claim.

Lukashenko told French magazineLe Pointin an interview published Wednesday that, “to say that (Ukraine’s) lands were Russian from ancient times … well, Russian lands, if you look deeper, were once Mongol-Tatar. Remember? So then, according to that logic, all of Russia should be given to whom – Mongolia?”

In the wide-ranging interview laced with falsehoods and inaccuracies that was otherwise largely supportive of Russia, Lukashenko told the magazine he believed Putin understood the logic was flawed, calling him a “shrewd, clever politician.”

Speaking to the French magazine, Lukashenko celebrated his friendship with Putin and repeated the Russian leader’s false narratives about Ukraine starting the war by “killing and burning Russian people.”

Lukashenko’s convictions, and close relationship with Putin, go back a long time. He was the only member of the Belarusian parliament who voted against the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. And, during his32 years as president, he has effectively turned Belarus into Russia’s vassal state.

Under his watch, Belarus has played a key role in the war in Ukraine. In February 2022, Lukashenko allowed Russia to use Belarus as a launching pad for Moscow’s full-scale invasion – even though he now denies knowing about it. Later, he agreed to host Russian tactical nuclear weapons.

“Putin and I can joke together, and we are all on informal, first-name terms with one another. He’s entirely approachable,” Lukashenko said, contrasting his relationship with Putin to that of US President Donald Trump’s relationship with the leaders of Western countries.

“You would never say such things to Trump. You sat around that table in Washington like parrots, afraid to say anything to him, sorry for putting it this way. He said whatever he wanted, even in a mocking manner. That is simply unacceptable among us,” he said.

Lukashenko also suggested he would be open to taking Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky to see Putin. “I could board a plane together and fly to Moscow. The two of us. As the guarantor of his security, I could sit down with him and fly to Moscow,” he said.

Addressing that suggestion, Zelensky dismissed it as “not serious.”

“We are at war, we cannot meet in Moscow, we cannot meet in Kyiv. We all understand this perfectly well. When someone says such things, it is simply not a serious conversation,” he said.

Lukashenko also said he believed Russia would eventually take over the entire eastern Ukrainian Donbas region, but he pushed back on some of Putin’s maximalist demands – such as the return of NATO’s borders to where they were in 1997.

“I am absolutely convinced that this is the start of negotiations. In any negotiations, both sides proceed from certain maximum conditions. But in the process of negotiations, one must sit at the table and negotiate,” Lukashenko told the publication.
